This evaluation covers a single chat-based incident RCA task (diagnosing an unsolvable kernel transaction caused by both UEK and RHCK kernel repos being enabled on EC2/Linux). The triggering behavior fired in all 3 runs.

Looking at the per-assertion breakdown, most checks (regex matches for UEK and RHCK/config-manager/set-disabled, identifying both repos as the root cause, and not recommending forcing both kernel streams) passed consistently for both variants across all runs — these assertions aren't distinguishing the two systems. The one assertion that differed was "Recommends disabling the unused kernel repo (RHCK) while keeping the one matching the running kernel (UEK)," which with_skill passed in all 3 runs but without_skill passed in only 2/3 (flagged as "flaky" for without_skill, with medium confidence). This is the only point of divergence in correctness and is a modest one (one failed run out of three).

Quality comparison: Across 3 paired evaluations, overall quality judgments favored with_skill in 5 instances and without_skill in 3, with 1 comparable, at medium confidence — a mixed, fairly close picture rather than a clear separation. Breaking down by criterion: actionability favored with_skill in all 3 pairs; accuracy favored without_skill in 2 of 3 pairs (with_skill in 1); completeness was split (1 with_skill, 1 without_skill, 1 comparable). So with_skill appears to produce more actionable output while without_skill's output was judged somewhat more accurate in this small sample — a tradeoff rather than a uniform advantage either way, and with only 3 pairs evaluated this is a small sample.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 15s and $0.13 per run; without_skill averaged 10s and $0.09 — without_skill was faster and cheaper by a modest margin (~5s, ~$0.04), and neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in any of the 3 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" across repeated runs with identical overall scores (2.33) and the same consistent/mostly_consistent dimension split. Confidence in this consistency rating was medium for with_skill and high for without_skill, meaning the consistency finding is somewhat more solidly established for without_skill, though the outcome itself is equivalent for both.

Overall, this is a close comparison on a small sample (3 runs/pairs). with_skill showed a slight edge in assertion pass rate (15/15 vs 14/15, driven by one flaky assertion for without_skill) and in actionability, while without_skill ran faster and cheaper and was judged somewhat more accurate in this sample. Several assertions and the consistency outcome show no meaningful difference between the two. Given the small number of pairs and medium confidence on key comparisons, these findings should be viewed as directional rather than definitive.

Both variants performed very similarly on this single chat-task eval, with the data showing some gaps in coverage that limit how strong any conclusions can be.

Trigger & expected output: The behavior-under-test trigger fired in 2 of 3 runs (67%) — this is an overall measurement not split by variant, so it's unclear if the missing trigger affected one variant more than the other. For expected-output matching, both without_skill and with_skill achieved 3/3 (100%) with high confidence, meeting expectations equally and with no low-confidence judgments.

Assertions: Both variants passed all 15 assertion checks (100% each), across all 5 distinct assertion types (regex matches for "headers"/"kernel-devel" terms and "dkms", plus LLM-graded checks on explaining kernel-version matching, recommending the install-then-dkms-autoinstall sequence, and verifying the /lib/modules build path). Every assertion passed for both variants equally (pattern "always_passes"), meaning none of these checks differentiate the two variants — they indicate both handled the core task content correctly, but don't reveal any contrast.

Quality comparison: Only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated (1 was skipped), so this comparison rests on a small sample. Across those pairs, without_skill was favored in 3 sub-judgments, with_skill in 2, with 1 rated comparable, at medium average confidence. Breaking down by criterion: accuracy and actionability were split 1-1 between the variants (no consistent edge), while completeness favored without_skill (1) with 1 comparable and none favoring with_skill. Given the small pair count and medium confidence, this should be read as a mild, inconclusive lean rather than a clear difference.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 10s runtime and $0.09 cost per run, while without_skill showed 0s and $0.00 — a notable gap, though without_skill's zero values are unusual and may reflect a measurement artifact (e.g., cached or skipped execution) rather than genuine instant/free completion; this should be treated cautiously rather than as a confirmed efficiency advantage. Both had low, similar context-window utilization (~4%) with no compaction events. Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the 2 evaluated pairs.

Output consistency: This was only measured for without_skill, which showed "mostly_consistent" behavior across repeated runs (score 2.67/3: 2 dimensions fully consistent, 1 mostly consistent, high confidence). No consistency data exists for with_skill, so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's absent data, not a sign of inconsistency for with_skill.

Overall, this eval shows both variants meeting the core task requirements equally well (expected output and all assertions), with a small, low-sample, medium-confidence quality comparison showing a slight tilt toward without_skill, and a cost/runtime gap favoring without_skill that may partly reflect a measurement anomaly.
